title: The restless mind
hookLine: Arjuna says the mind is restless as the wind; Krishna: practice and detachment tame it (Bhagavad Gita 6.34–35)
tomorrow: what are the seven verses said in every Muslim prayer?

lines: AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.
cards: Ten seconds into a meditation app, and the mind is already planning dinner. There's company for that in an old place. In chapter six, after Krishna has described the seat and the steady mind, Arjuna pushes back.
This evenness you teach, he says, I can't see how it lasts. The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind.

teach.b: Two sides, and the Gita lets both speak. Arjuna's case is strong. He isn't lazy; he's honest.
He has watched his own mind, and it moves like weather. A teaching that only works for a calm mind, he's saying, doesn't help the person who needs it most.
Krishna doesn't fight that. His first word is a concession: doubtless, the mind is restless and hard to hold. Then his answer: it is held by practice, and by letting go.
The Sanskrit pair is abhyasa and vairagya.
Abhyasa is coming back to the same place, again and again; a few verses earlier Krishna says, wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back.
Vairagya is loosening the grip of wanting, so there's less pulling the mind away.
Then Krishna keeps Arjuna's point alive: for one without self-control, he says, this yoga is hard to reach; for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. So who wins?
In the text, neither side is erased. Arjuna names a problem nobody can wave away; Krishna names the slow road through it.
And one more thread: the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, a separate Hindu text on stilling the mind, use the very same pair.

how: Hindu teachers of meditation draw on Gita 6.35 and on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, where practice and letting go are named together as the way the mind is stilled.

o: a mind ruined for good by too much worry and noise
a mind that won't settle, held by practice and letting go
a mind that's sharp because it never stops moving

games.q: the debate in chapter six: tap the pairs.
p: the mind is restless as the wind
doubtless; and yet it can be held
practice: coming back again and again

s: in the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna the mind is easy to calm
his first word is a concession: doubtless, it is restless and hard to hold.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras use the same pair, practice and letting go
the Yoga Sutras name abhyasa and vairagya for stilling the mind.
if your mind wanders, the meditation has failed
in Gita 6.26, bringing the wandering mind back is the practice itself.

games.q: a friend says the Gita's answer is too easy, because some minds really can't settle. what's the best case for her side, from the Gita itself?
o: Arjuna said it first: the mind is as hard to hold as wind, and Krishna agreed.
there isn't one; Krishna shows any mind goes calm in one sitting.
the Gita never admits the mind is hard; she has misread it.
games.why: Krishna's first word is doubtless: he grants Arjuna's point before he names practice and letting go.

practice: Close your eyes and rest your attention on the breath where it enters the nose. When the mind wanders, and it will, that's the practice: notice it, let the thought go without chasing it, and come back. Every return counts.

wordCard.voice: The restless mind: Arjuna's wind, and Krishna's two-handed answer, abhyasa and vairagya.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 6.35: abhyasa, practice, paired with vairagya, letting go.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: practice and letting go, both hands on the wind. That's the Gita, six of six.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.33–34 (Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to control as the wind)

Bhagavad Gita 6.35–36 (Krishna: doubtless the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it is held by practice and dispassion; hard for the uncontrolled, attainable for the one who strives by right means)
Bhagavad Gita 6.26 (wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back)
Patanjali, Yoga Sutras 1.12 (the stilling of the mind comes by practice and non-attachment, abhyasa and vairagya)
